content.summary_of_the_paper: This study proposed a neural integral equation, which approximates integral equation based on the Adomian Decomposition Method; it can solve an ODE faster than ordinary numerical solver. Moreover, it proposes an attentional neural integral equation, which replaces the integration in integral equation with an attentional component, and accelerates the integration, achieving the fact computation and remarkably accurate prediction of PDEs from data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

This study proposes a neural integral equation, which learns integral equations from data. Thed problem setting is important and clearly stated.

The experimental results are remarkable. The data-driven modeling and fast computation of PDEs contribute to science and engineering much. This study provides a good improvement.

**Weakness**

*Justification:*

In my understanding, Algorithm 1 is not totally the same as the Adomian Decomposition Method introduced in Section 4.2.1, Wazwaz (2011), which gives the solution $y$ as the sum of infinite series $y_1,y_2,\dots$ under the assumption that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are independent of $t$ (that is, Fredholm), $f$ is independent of $y$, and $F$ is linear. It is needed to specify the section or reference that introduces Algorithm 1 or bridge the gap by authors.

Moreover, it would be better to clarify the conditions under which Algorithm 1 converges, for a randomly initialized neural network.

Also, it is unclear whether the neural network learns properly by minimizing the error between $y(t)$ and the observations. Algorithms are iterative, so what kind of computation graph is stored? Is this something more than a deep learning magic?

"operator learning" means the replacement of the integral with Att network in Algorithm 2. I found it after reading the manuscript twice. Please state this fact in Section 2.2, where "operator learning" does not appear once. This approach is interesting, but the rationale is unclear. Is this just a brute-force using deep learning or a reasonable approximation? Please specify.

*Novelty:*

The authors stated in Introduction that

> known methods require that the integral operator that determines the IE is known, and given. Instead, in our approach we learn the integral operator itself, and therefore an integral equation, from observations alone.

and I found several previous studies are similar to the NIE. Is the main novelty of this manuscript the ANIE proposal? Or is there novelty in the NIE as well?

*Comparison:*

Latent neural ODE is compared in Table 1, but why not neural ODE (without input) or neural controlled ODE (with input)?

=============
*After discussion*

Thanks to reviewer 4o9i's comments, I have noticed that the contributions were overestimated and that many of them are actually due to existing studies. My initial score was based on my ignorance, for which I apologize.

I still believe that as long as the self-attention is a useful approximation, it need not be a theoretically valid approximation of the integral. Hence, I would like to change my score from 6 to 5.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:

Reproducibility: It would be better to clarity the attention procedure used in ANIE and its possible alternatives. While the source code is provided, a manuscript should be self-explanatory. content.summary_of_the_review: I think the proposal is based on good ideas and solid theory, but some parts are not explained well enough. My main concern includes "whether NIE is certainly novel" and "whether ANIE can be theoretically supported". I do not find other critical flaws.

content.title: Comments to reviewer RirC
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for providing their constructive insight. 

Comment from the reviewer: “​​In my understanding, Algorithm 1 is not totally the same as the Adomian Decomposition Method introduced in Section 4.2.1, Wazwaz (2011), which gives the solution y as the sum of infinite series y1,y2,… under the assumption that α and β  are independent of t (that is, Fredholm), f is independent of y, and F is linear. It is needed to specify the section or reference that introduces Algorithm 1 or bridge the gap by authors.”

The algorithm given by Wazwaz in section 4.2.1 of the book is a highly simplified version of the general procedure. The iterative algorithms used in our article are employed at great lengths in computational physics and mathematics and are known to be applicable in general. We could refer to more references, if the reviewer deems it useful.

Comment from the reviewer: “Moreover, it would be better to clarify the conditions under which Algorithm 1 converges, for a randomly initialized neural network.”

Regarding the convergence of Algorithm 1. The conditions for the algorithm to converge are found in the literature. We can add some more specific comments in this regard pointing more clearly to some of the references that are less elementary than Wazwaz. The fact that the neural network is randomly initialized is not indeed an issue, as integrability only is required, which is guaranteed by the intrinsic smoothness of the neural network.

Comment from the reviewer: “Also, it is unclear whether the neural network learns properly by minimizing the error between y(t)  and the observations. Algorithms are iterative, so what kind of computation graph is stored? Is this something more than a deep learning magic?

This is a good point. We have two schemes for the computational graph in the backpropagation of Algorithm 2. One where we save the gradients at each evaluation of the iteration, and one where the evaluation happens only on the last step. We can add these details in the article. Thank you for pointing this out.

Comment from the reviewer: “operator learning" means the replacement of the integral with Att network in Algorithm 2. I found it after reading the manuscript twice. Please state this fact in Section 2.2, where "operator learning" does not appear once. This approach is interesting, but the rationale is unclear. Is this just a brute-force using deep learning or a reasonable approximation? Please specify.”

Algorithm 1 is also an operator learning problem, since we learn the underlying integral operator of the equation. So, the term does not refer to the passage from the framework of Algorithm 1 to that of Algorithm 2. Here operator learning refers to the fact that the model takes as input a function, and outputs a function, which is what usually is referred to as “Operator”, in mathematical analysis and theoretical physics. We will make this clearer throughout the manuscript.

Comment from the reviewer: “The authors stated in Introduction that “known methods require that the integral operator that determines the IE is known, and given. Instead, in our approach we learn the integral operator itself, and therefore an integral equation, from observations alone.” , and I found several previous studies are similar to the NIE. Is the main novelty of this manuscript the ANIE proposal? Or is there novelty in the NIE as well?”

The novelty of NIE is quite significant, as there are no other frameworks for learning the integral operator of an integral equation. All previous methods were mostly targeting the solution of certain types of integral equations, e.g. Fredholm. In other words, they learn the solutions, rather than the operator itself. The two perspectives are different. For instance, taking the Navier-Stokes setting as an example. Previous models could find solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations once the system is understood to be of Navier-Stokes type. In our model, we have a dataset produced from Navier-Stokes, but the model has no knowledge of the underlying system that generates the data. It learns the Navier-Stokes operator in integral form. The use of attention is well motivated from the references that have shown that transformers perform a computationally efficient integral over their input. Thus, both NIE and ANIE constitute significant and fundamental novelty in the field.

Comment from the reviewer: “Latent neural ODE is compared in Table 1, but why not neural ODE (without input) or neural controlled ODE (with input)?”

In our training speed experiments, we have used the architecture described by the authors of NODE for the same family of dynamical systems we used in section 3.1 of our manuscript. In NODE, the authors introduced the Latent ODE as a way to encode the full dynamics via a reverse RNN to an initial condition before applying their solver. We will include training speed also for the simple NODE in a revised version of the manuscript.

content.title: Comments to reviewer Jt6d
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback. 

Comment from the reviewer: “This paper introduces a notion of (neural) “integral equations” as effectively generalised competitor to neural ODEs.”

The overview statement is profoundly underestimating the contribution intended by this article. Our objective is not to extend ODE models, but to provide a framework for integral equations in deep learning. As a byproduct we also obtain a generalization of ODE models since integral equations greatly generalize ODEs. This provides a faster and more stable ODE solver. However, our work fundamentally goes beyond ODEs, as we also extend PDE based models, and, perhaps most importantly, we introduce a completely new operator learning framework for Integral Equations. 

Comment from the reviewer: “results have lots of promise, but are mixed”

On Navier-Stokes systems we surpass the state-of-the-art model (FNO) by one order of magnitude. We systematically show superior performance on several other systems. It is not clear to us how this is a “mixed result”.

Comment from the reviewer: “poor writing and presentation: citations are missing,”

Where specifically? To the best of our knowledge, no citations are missing. We would gladly incorporate any specific suggestions.

Comment from the reviewer: “notation is sloppy, math is often undefined or unclear”

Where specifically? To the best of our ability, we have provided clear mathematical notation. We would gladly incorporate any specific suggestions.

Comment from the reviewer: “tables are poorly formatted”

We thank the reviewer for the comment. We will address that on a revised version of the manuscript. We would gladly incorporate any specific suggestions.

Comment from the reviewer: “the motivations or explanations of the method are weak, etc. w: little method novelty: the paper throws in attention.”

We have introduced a completely novel integral operator learning framework. No such method existed yet. The state of the art were PDE modeling approaches (e.g. FNO). We systematically showed superior performance in ODE, PDE, and IE systems. We do not understand why this is “little method novelty”.

We clearly explain in the paper that we employ self-attention as an integration method to allow for better performance as well as integration in arbitrary space dimensions. Our base model (NIE) makes use of Monte Carlo integration, which, as we explain, does not scale well. We used attention since in prior literature it was established that attention implements a Nystrom approximation of the integral operator. Various references have been given in this regard. Thus, we gave clear reasons and explanations for using attention in the model.

Comment from the reviewer: “There is not even an attempt to develop a principled model for the IE framework.”

We presented a new framework for integral operator learning. We provide the mathematical foundations and algorithms for our approach. We are happy to incorporate any specific comments on our method.

Comment from the reviewer: “w: it's unclear what happens: The method is not opened up, or shown what is being learned. Fig3 does show what's going on, but the result is quite strange: we have the same bad-looking attention map 4 times. It doesn't look like the method is working correctly, or that it makes much sense.”

We have provided the algorithms used to implement our integral equations solver. These were based on a very solid theory that has been known for over a century. It is not clear to us how this does not account as “opening up” the model. The model learns an integral operator, as stated several times in the manuscript. The actual form of the operator learned, depends on the system. We are unclear why the attention map in Fig 3 is considered as being “bad-looking”. The 4 plots correspond to 4 attention heads, which show similar (but not identical) patterns.

We are happy to improve our manuscript with specific comments if the reviewer can provide these.

content.comment:
The first problem this paper has is to motivate, introduce and explain to the reader what are IEs, both conceptually and technically. After reading sec 2 several times, I still don’t understand what IEs are, or why should we care about them. I think the paper assumes that reader already knows about them, but that’s a bold assumption for a machine learning conference. One problem here is sloppy presentation: y,f are undefined, G is initially undefined (turns into kernel later), role of s/t is unclear, role of a/b is unclear, role of y/f is unclear, F is undefined. Fredholm/Volterra are unexplained, and connection to PDEs or ODEs is not clear (is there a dy/dt somewhere? Should there be?). The attention is undefined.

The results are mixed because in some cases there is improvement, in some cases there is not.

The method is not "opened up”, because it is not explained what the neural networks learn to do in practise. The head visualisation could help, but I can't interpret what fig3 means. It seems bottom left is concentrated, not sure what does that mean. Also not sure what do attention weights mean, or how they relate to the rest of the system (eg. F or K or y or keys or queries).

content.title: Comments to reviewer 4o9i - Part 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. We believe that this review overlooks significant portions of our work. We respectfully want to point out a number of incorrect facts stated in this review.

The reviewer writes: “did an integral over time”.

This does not reflect what we did. Throughout the article we state that our method integrates over both space and time. Moreover, several of our applications are PDEs, which have explicit space dependencies and are thus solved with space integration. Thus, it appears that the reviewer did not notice one of our main contributions, which is spatiotemporal integration in arbitrary dimensions. The reviewer only mentions ODEs (time integration) and does not refer to PDEs (space+time integration).


Comment from reviewer: “Weakness: 1.The experiment did in 2d-trajectory are all markovian systems. The improvement of this model beyond NODE is not explained as the motivation proposed. At the same time, it's also worse than LSTM.”

In this experiment, a markovian (ODE) system was chosen on purpose in order to demonstrate the improved performance (training speed) of our model compared to NODE. More complex systems (e.g. PDEs) can not even be modeled with NODE and thus ODE systems are required for this specific comparison. LSTM was included as it is known to be very fast, but is incapable of modeling continuous dynamics, as is demonstrated in the NODE paper. Our point, which we clearly state, is that our model outperforms other continuous dynamics approaches (NODE) and has the same fast training speed as LSTMs which can not model continuous data. Our model is therefore “best of both worlds” - continuous as well as fast. The motivation of this experiment was clearly described and our results clearly show our contribution.


Comment from reviewer: “The author haven't show why self-attention is a good approximation to the integral equation”

In our manuscript, we have referred to various articles that have shown that self-attention can be interpreted as performing an integration (Cao 2021, Xiong et al., 2021). These articles are given in the last paragraph of section 1, and in section 2.2. Consequently, the integral operator in an integral equation can be approximated via self-attention.

Comment from reviewer: “I don't think after an attention approximation, it's a continuous time model”

As we explain in the manuscript, our model is an integral equation solver based on the Adomian decomposition method. This gives a continuous time and space model. We implemented several different integration methods. The self-attention approximation of integration is used in one version of the model, but does not change anything about the continuous nature of the model. In fact, in previous literature (Cao, 2021; Xiong et al., 2021) it was shown (and proven) that self-attention is a Nystrom approximation of an integral operator. Integral equations are continuous by definition, regardless of the numerical scheme adopted to perform the integration (e.g. Monte Carlo or self-attention).

Comment from reviewer: “what is the benefit of a continuous time model?”

We are puzzled by this comment. Many physical systems are continuous in nature and as a result, for centuries, humanity has tried to understand these systems with continuous models. ODEs and PDEs are fundamentally continuous models and have extensively been used to model nature. Data is often discretely sampled but the underlying system is continuous. There is a long list of reasons why one would model discretely sampled data with continuous models - the NODE paper describes a number of them, for example modeling irregularly sampled data such as hospital visits. In our manuscript we consider several continuous systems, such as brain dynamics and fluid flow.

Comment from reviewer: “In NODE paper, they deal with generative modeling. The continuous time model provides nature invertibility and tractable computation of log(det). I don't know the benefit of continuous here for regression.”

This refers to continuous normalizing flows, which is only one of several applications of NODE. This is not the Neural ODE application we consider. We do not understand why the reviewer mentions this model. The NODE paper clearly describes their motivations for continuous time modeling.

Comment from the reviewer: “The author should also select a naive discretization of the NIE first then use the self-attention”

While integral equations are continuous, any integral equation solver uses a discrete approximation scheme since computers are fundamentally discrete machines. Thus, both NIE and ANIE use discrete schemes for solving the integral equations. As described in the manuscript, NIE uses Monte Carlo integration (via Torchquad) and ANIE uses self-attention.

replying_to: Replying to Comments to reviewer 4o9i - Part 1

content.title: Comments to reviewer 4o9i - Part 2
content.comment:
Comment from the reviewer: “(I can't find any detail about the scheme used for NIE on 2d trajectory data.)”

There is no discretization scheme, as the data is discretely generated. As described in the manuscript, the input of the model are samples of the data in time or space+time, depending on ODE or PDE modeling, respectively.


Comment from the reviewer: “At the same time, NIE result on FMRI is not reported. I still do not believe the improvement is because of the integral equation modeling.”

We did not include NIE because it does not allow for efficient space integration, as we describe in the manuscript. ANIE was designed, as we described, to allow for efficient integration in time plus arbitrary space dimensions. Since fMRI data is spatiotemporal, it requires modeling in time and space and thus ANIE was used to model it.

We do not understand why the reviewer does “not believe the improvement” because we systematically benchmark ANIE and compare it quantitatively to other methods. We have formulated the problem using integral equations and solved it. This is a widely employed approach in computational physics and mathematics that we have implemented with a novel neural integral equation that uses self-attention for efficient integration.


Comment from the reviewer: “I even think LSTM can approximate an Integral equation. I think it's easy to construct a numerical scheme of the IE is a special case of the LSTM.”

This statement is factually wrong. LSTMs are sequential, in that they produce an output for a time point using previous outputs. This is comparable to having a delay differential equation. In the case of convolutional LSTMs (which we have used for comparison on Burgers’ and Navier-Stokes equations) this could be compared to a partial delay differential equation. However, (partial) delay differential equations are known to NOT be equivalent to integral equations, so the reviewer is suggesting that 200 years of results in mathematics are wrong. 
The fundamental difference resides in the fact that the iterative procedure used to solve integral equations (where all the time points are used at each iteration), and the sequential procedure used in LSTMs, where some points in the past are used to produce future points in time, are substantially not equivalent. 


Comment from the reviewer: “What is the scheme used for NODE baseline?”

We have described how the training procedure has been performed for all models. See for instance section 3.5 for a specific description of the NODE baseline scheme. 


Comment from the reviewer: “The paper prosed an interesting way to use attention to formulate the memory of a time series”

As is described in the manuscript, we model an integral equation which is not at all “memory of a time series”. We integrate in continuous space and time. ODEs, PDEs, and IEs can not be reduced to time series. Hundreds of years of mathematics have established this.

In addition, a “time series” is a type of data. This can come from all kinds of underlying systems, discrete or continuous. Having “time series” data does not determine by definition how to model this data, e.g. with an ODE (continuous) or with an LSTM (discrete). This should depend on the goals of the model. In our paper we have sampled data from continuous systems with the goal to model these with continuous models.


Comment from the reviewer: “The author hasn't provided evidence that the improvement is because of the IE modeling”

Integral equation solvers are widely employed in numerical analysis, and they have been shown to be more efficient than ODE and PDE solvers (to solve ODEs and PDEs), as the two references by Rokhlin cited in our manuscript clearly show. Moreover, Integral equation systems, e.g. with non-local spatial interactions, should be solved with IE solvers. Our contribution is a neural network based model that learns and solves an integral equation from data. Our model outperforms several other methods on ODE and PDE systems. We do not understand why the reviewer thinks that this does not constitute evidence that the improvement is because of IE modeling.

content.title: Comments to the second answer
content.comment:
We would only like to clarify very few facts, and point out a persistent error in the reviewer’s perspective. We understand that the reviewer does not “believe” in several of the articles that we have cited, using their own wording. We would like to specify that we are not interested in changing the reviewer’s beliefs. 

Comment from reviewer: “you claim is totally wrong. I can easily turns an integral equation x_t+1 = a_0x_t+.... a_s x_t-f(x_t) as a sequential model via using (x_t+1,x_t,...,x_t-s+1) as latent space. This is exactly how LSTM to encode memory.” 

An integral equation is not a sequence of points, to be precise, but this is not the issue at hand. The main flaw in this argument is that it is believed that integral equations only encode memory, which is a fact we disputed already. For simplicity, let us consider an integral equation with only time dependence, and therefore no space. Also, just to fix notation we use Fredholm integral equations in the interval $0$ to $1$. 
An integral equation has a solution $y$ whose evaluation at time $t$ satisfies the equation
$$y(t) = \int _0^1 G(y,t,s)ds$$. As it is easily seen, in order to compute $y$ at $t$, one needs the value of $y$ on the whole interval $[0,1,]$. The scheme given above, only uses points before $t+1$ to compute the evaluation of $y$ at $t+1$. This is absolutely incorrect, as it is very easy to see from our very simple argument, and it is the reason why every book and reference in integral equations mentions iterative procedures as opposed to sequential procedures. Integral equations encode memory, as well as present and future, as it is well known and easily understood from the defining equations.


Comment from reviewer: “Because you can't prove your network can approximate an integral equation. Plz write it down as a theorem.
At the same time, the 2d data is generated by an ODE, your network still provides an improvement. Can give me any reference that integral equation do a better approximation than ODE even when the ground truth data is generated by an ODE?” 

Actually, using the results from the Nystromformer paper and Cao’s paper, there is not much to be proved, since those results substantially apply here. There is no theorem to consider in this case. Maybe a clarifying statement, at most. The main issue here seems that the reviewer does not ”believe” those papers, in which case there is not much we can do. Once again, it is not our intention to change anyone’s beliefs. Regarding the requested references, the two articles by Rokhlin that we cited and that we mentioned in previous answers show this to a deep extent in the case of PDE systems. For ODE systems the result is similar and even older. We truly hope that these articles do not hurt the reviewer’s beliefs, and that they find them agreeable.

content.title: Runge-Kutta
content.comment:
Runge-Kutte is sequential. Integral equation solvers are iterative.

In an integral equation solver one initializes the solver with a function (say a whole function on the interval [0,1]). This is a solution to the equation, but usually a poor one. Then the integral operator is applied to it (since we have the whole function we can integrate over the whole interval [0,1]) and the output summed to the previous initialization. Usually here one can choose a smoothing factor. In our case this was 1/2. This is repeated until convergence happens (following the references given above).

In a Runge-Kutta scheme (whatever variation) one solves the linear system of equations which are localized in time. And sequentially does this for the whole interval. The catch here is the iterative procedure vs. the sequential procedure.

The improvement on Lotka-Volterra is just speed. We mention that all the models can fit the data, but our model is as fast as an LSTM (roughly), but faster than an ode solver. For the well-posedness. Under relatively mild conditions IEs admit a unique solution. The references we gave in the appendix have several theorems for the well-posedness of IEs. We would only like to point out that this is the same with deep learning models with ODE systems.
